body:
Last night’s show started with California.
Which, admittedly, sounds like punishment.
But California politics is actually a perfect prediction market laboratory because the incentives are so obvious once you stop listening to the speeches and start watching the behavior.
That’s the key distinction.
Narratives tell you what politicians want you to believe.

Markets tell you what people think is actually going to happen.
And those are often two very different things.
The biggest example right now is the California governor’s race.
A few months ago, Eric Swalwell was treated like a serious contender. Markets had him near the top of the field at one point. Then everything collapsed.
Now, the media version of the story is scandal, controversy, inappropriate behavior, and Democrats suddenly discovering moral standards they forgot existed for the past decade.
I don’t buy that for one second.
Because if California Democrats truly cared about the behavior itself, they would have cared long before the polling and market dynamics became dangerous.
The actual reason Swalwell disappeared is much more predictable:
Democrats became terrified of splitting the vote badly enough to accidentally create a Republican-vs-Republican final election scenario.
That’s it.
That’s the story.
Not morality. Not accountability. Not principle.
Just incentives.
And once you understand that, the rest of the race suddenly makes a lot more sense.
For example, last night we walked through the collapse of Katie Porter, who somehow managed to go from major contender to sitting around 1% territory in the markets.
One percent.
That’s basically prediction-market hospice care.
And honestly? The markets may still be generous.
We played one of my favorite games on the show: “Predict the Prediction.”
Before looking at the market price, you just watch the candidate. Listen to the debate clips. Observe the incentives. Then guess where you think the market 
should
 be.
It’s one of the best ways to train yourself to spot value.
Because when your internal number and the market number wildly disagree, that’s where opportunity starts to appear.
Sometimes the market is wrong.
Sometimes 
you’re
 wrong.
The important part is learning why.
We also got into why Xavier Becerra is suddenly emerging as the “safe” option for nervous Democrats, why Republicans still face an uphill climb even in a chaotic field, and the surprisingly real path for Steve Hilton to outperform expectations.
And yes, we talked about the British accent advantage.
Because if you sound smarter, you probably gain at least three points automatically.
That’s just science.
We also dug into the Los Angeles mayor race, where Spencer Pratt may actually be running a more competent campaign than half the professional political class.
Again: incentives.
A guy whose house burned down campaigning against the people who failed to stop the city from burning down is a much stronger message than consultants usually realize.
But honestly, the most important segment of the night may have been the one on rules.
Not the exciting part. Not the viral part.
The useful part.
Because prediction markets are full of people who think they understand what a contract means… right up until it resolves against them.
We walked through an Iran nuclear deal market that looks straightforward on the surface but becomes a completely different bet once you actually read the resolution criteria carefully.
That’s where a lot of people get destroyed.
Not because they misunderstood the news.
Because they misunderstood the contract.
Huge difference.
We also hit the DOJ investigation into billions of dollars of suspicious oil trades surrounding Iran-related announcements, which is particularly interesting considering how often prediction markets get singled out while traditional financial markets quietly move astronomical amounts of money around geopolitical events.
Funny how that works.
Anyway, there was a lot in this one.
California panic.

Market psychology.

Political incentives.

Oil trades.

Nuclear deal rules.

And one particular governor’s race setup that could become much more chaotic than people currently realize.
Especially if a certain 7% scenario starts creeping upward.
That’s where things get interesting.
